segments.say: So does it work. Every engineer on that team was told to write their own unit tests, and here is what they wrote. A hundred and nineteen tests. A hundred and eighteen pass. One skipped, none failed, and the whole suite runs in about a third of a second. If you have been sold agent teams by somebody's launch video, this is the frame where the video ends. Green ticks, a round number, roll credits. Be more suspicious than that. Read the names as they go past, because the names are the only claim being made here. The simulator keeps its own clock. Late vehicles sort to the top of their group. Colour runs green to red as risk climbs. Real behaviours, and if they are genuinely pinned, this suite is worth something. And notice who wrote them. There was no testing agent on this team. I split the work six ways by layer and by feature, and every engineer was told to test their own piece, because the person who wrote the tick logic is the person who knows what would quietly break it.

That decision is about to be examined, because a suite written by the same six people who wrote the code has one obvious failure mode: everybody grades their own homework. But a green suite is not evidence on its own. A test that cannot fail is not a test, it is a comment that takes time to run. So rather than admire the number, I am going to ask the harder question, and I am going to ask it in a way that makes it difficult to answer politely. How many tests, how many pass, and the question that actually matters: would these tests fail if the behaviour were wrong? Pick the two weakest tests in the suite and show me why they are weak. And then, deliberately: do not fix anything yet. That last clause is doing real work. If you let it diagnose and repair in one breath you will never see the diagnosis — it will scroll past under a patch, and you will be reviewing a fix for a problem you were never shown. Separate the two. Look at what comes back, because it is more specific than I expected. Weakest test number one asserts that the dispatcher returned status two hundred, that the reply is a non-empty string, and that the actions field is an array. It never looks at what the reply says. And the agent proves the point rather than asserting it: swap the dispatcher's real answer for the word okay and an empty list, and this test still passes. It is testing that the HTTP plumbing exists, not that the chat answers questions. And I want to be fair to whichever teammate wrote it, because this is not laziness, it is the most natural mistake in the trade. When you are building a route and you want to know it is wired up, you assert the shape of what comes back. It passes, you move on, and the test stays there forever looking like coverage. Every codebase you have ever worked in has tests like this in it. The difference here is that there are a hundred and nineteen of them written in eight minutes, so whatever habit the model has, you now have it at scale, and you find out which habit that is by asking rather than by waiting for production to tell you.

Weakest test number two is worse, because the name lies. The test is called stats phrasing variants all answer with delivery figures, and it sounds thorough. The assertion underneath it is a case-insensitive search for the word deliver anywhere in the reply. We deliver on time would pass it. No risky lane data would pass its sibling. No percentage is checked, no lane is named, nothing is ranked. And the agent is careful to say this is a real gap rather than a hypothetical one, because a few lines up in the very same file two other tests do it correctly — they read the actual simulator state and assert against a value computed from it. So the weak version is redundant beside a real check, and taken on its own it would not catch a broken handler. Then it names the pattern both failures share, and this is the sentence to take away from the whole lecture. Both assert on the type or the presence of output — it is a string, it contains a word — instead of asserting on a value computed from real state. It contains this vehicle's actual ETA. It contains this region's actual risk score. That distinction is the difference between a suite that protects you and a suite that only makes you feel protected. Now the second instruction: fix only what is genuinely broken. Code, not tests. And if a test is wrong rather than the code, say so, change the test, and tell me which you did. Watch what comes back, because it does not do what I half expected. Nothing in the code was broken. It traced the real handlers behind both weak spots, exercised them against a live simulator, and the numbers came back correct — the on-time rate matched the simulator exactly, the risk ranking matched the lane ordering exactly. Eighty-seven percent on time, four hundred and six of four hundred and sixty-eight, sixty-two late — matching what the simulator held. It exercised the real handlers rather than reading them — the only way that answer is worth anything. So the code was right and the tests were wrong. It rewrote both of them to compute the expected value from the same simulator instance first, and then assert against that grounded number instead of a substring. A hundred and nineteen tests, a hundred and eighteen pass, one skipped — the same as before. And that identical number now means something completely different. Before, it meant the tests ran. Now it means the behaviour underneath them is genuinely correct. That is what an integration pass is actually for, and no green tick would have told you the difference. So take three things out of this lecture. First, the review step is not optional, and it is not the same as running the suite. Running the suite tells you the tests pass. Only reading them tells you whether passing means anything. Second, split diagnosis from repair, every time. The instruction do not fix anything yet costs you one extra turn and it buys you the entire reasoning, in your own hands, before a patch hides it. If you merge those two steps you will spend the rest of the project trusting summaries. And third, notice that the honest answer here was nothing in the code was broken. That is an answer an agent has to be given permission to give. If you ask it to fix the failures, it will find failures, because you told it there were some — and it will rewrite working code to satisfy a badly written test. I asked it to fix only what is genuinely broken, to say so if the test was wrong instead, and to tell me which of the two it had done. Every one of those clauses is load bearing. That is the whole skill, and it is not a coding skill. It is knowing which question closes the door on a comfortable answer.
